The basset clarinet is an aerophone of the clarinet family, Hornbostel–Sachs 422.211.2. It resembles an ordinary soprano clarinet but has a longer body, 18 centimetres longer in total than an ordinary clarinet, and extra keys that extend the range downwards, usually to written C or B instead of the E or E-flat of the standard clarinet. It is mostly played with Boehm fingering, and is commonly a transposing instrument in A, with C, B-flat and rarely G versions as well. It is known because Mozart wrote the Clarinet Quintet, the Clarinet Concerto and the aria in La clemenza di Tito for Anton Stadler; today it also appears in classical concertos, chamber music, opera and free jazz.
巴塞單簧管為氣鳴木管樂器，音色與一般單簧管無異。其管身較長並增設鍵位，使音域比普: The basset clarinet is an aerophone of woodwind type, and its timbre is no different from an ordinary clarinet's. Its body is longer and carries extra keys, extending the range four or five semitones below an ordinary clarinet; the written range runs from low C or low B to C7, four octaves. It is commonly a transposing instrument in A, with C, B-flat and G versions as well. Different bell shapes and directions affect the sound. The source does not mention how volume is controlled.
最早現存巴塞單簧管可追溯至1770年，見於巴黎與倫敦博物館。約1788年，維也納: The earliest surviving basset clarinet dates from 1770 and is held in museums in Paris and London. Around 1788 the Viennese court instrument maker Theodor Lotz made one for Anton Stadler; a concert programme from Riga in 1794 preserves a drawing of the instrument, and the name is found by 1796. Mozart's Clarinet Quintet, Clarinet Concerto and the opera La clemenza di Tito are all connected with it. Only a few were made from the nineteenth century to the early twentieth, mostly for playing Mozart; after the mid-twentieth century interest in historical performance revived it, modern composers have written for it, and an extension joint has appeared that lets an ordinary clarinet be converted.
